verses.note: In Israel the offices of king and priest were kept apart, and kings who took priestly roles were rebuked (2 Chronicles 26:16-18). Melchizedek holds both at once, which is why Scripture can use him to describe the Messiah's joined kingship and priesthood.

The first person Scripture calls a prophet is Abraham, and what defines him here is not prediction but nearness to God and the right to plead for others. That shape of the prophetic office runs through the Old Testament and is fulfilled in Christ, who always lives to intercede (Hebrews 7:25).

Aaron's marriage joins the priestly line to the house of Nahshon, whose descendant David will found Israel's royal line (Ruth 4:20-22; Matthew 1:4-6). The Old Testament keeps the offices of priest and king separate, but the two families are joined here; the New Testament presents Jesus as fulfilling both offices (Hebrews 7:14-17).

Moses stands between God and the people as prophet, speaking God's words to them. Deuteronomy 18:15-18 remembers this request as the origin of the prophetic office and promises a prophet like Moses, whom the New Testament identifies with Jesus (Acts 3:22-23).

Moses mediates God's words to the people as he did at the first giving of the law. The fear his face provokes is the same fear the people felt at God's voice (20:19), and it is answered the same way: God's word comes to them through the mediator.

On this one day the high priest sets aside the gold and jewels of his office (Exodus 28) and enters in plain linen. His representative role is most complete when his personal splendor is removed, and he must first deal with his own sin before he can act for others.
The mediator acts alone, unseen, on behalf of all. Hebrews reads Christ's work in these terms: he entered the true sanctuary alone and appears there on our behalf (Hebrews 9:24).

The high priest's office passes from father to son, and each dies in turn. Hebrews builds its argument on this: the former priests were many because death prevented them from continuing, but Jesus holds his priesthood permanently because he lives forever (Hebrews 7:23-25).
The priesthood is set apart from the ordinary economy of land and inheritance. Those who serve at the altar are meant to depend on God and on the worship of his people, not on estates of their own.

Christian theology has named prophet as one of Christ's three offices, with priest and king. Jesus' claim in John 12:49-50 that he speaks just what the Father commanded him echoes the language of this verse.

The verse joins kingship and priesthood in one person by divine oath. The church's teaching that Christ holds the offices of prophet, priest, and king (set out at length by Calvin, Institutes 2.15) finds one of its main Old Testament roots here.

Jesus blesses his people as a priest and is taken up to heaven, where, as Hebrews says, he lives to intercede for them (Hebrews 7:25). The church has spoken of Christ's threefold office as prophet, priest, and king; Luke's last picture shows the priest whose blessing continues from heaven.
